newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan traders not nervous over Gecamines directive.
newsitem.headline: Japan traders not nervous over Gecamines directive.

text.p: Japanese cobalt traders said on Monday they were little worried by a recent Gecamines circular that prompted concerns in Europe that the state-owned Zairean producer might not honour some of its existing contracts.
"We won't see as much impact as in Europe or North America. The proportion of term contracts is not large. It's less than half (of Japan's consumption of Zairean cobalt)," one trader said.

Gecamines, which was recently taken over by Laurent Kabila's rebels, last week sent customers a circular that triggered concerns the new management was looking to renegotiate contracts on terms more favourable to the seller.

According to data compiled by Mitsui & Co Ltd, one of Gecamines' agents in Japan, Japanese imports of cobalt from Zaire and Zambia totalled about 2,600 tonnes in 1996, roughly half of Japan's total imports of the metal.
Japanese traders said that in Tokyo on Monday high-grade cobalt was quoted steady at $25.50 per lb while low-grade was at $22.50.

"The (Gecamines) news might have a psychological impact and raise the metal's price, but Gecamines cannot change the amount of high-grade cobalt supplied to the market," said a trader at a major Japanese trading house.
He said Gecamines had stopped producing high-grade cobalt five years ago, although there was still Zairean high-grade metal in the market that had been produced before that time.
Another trader said he expected Gecamines to resume spot cobalt sales this week after informing customers of a resumption last week.
Traders here agreed that the metal's price was unlikely to climb further as Zaire's political turmoil was nearing its end following the departure of president Mobutu Sese Seko.
"People must be relieved over the political conclusion (in Zaire)," said one trader. "The metal's price is going to stabilise for the time being."
